title: The real campus behind the Whale campaign
body: A major social media company is building a multi-building AI data center campus on roughly 2,250 acres in a rural Louisiana parish, with plans to grow it toward 5 gigawatts and tens of billions of dollars of investment. The campaign's four-hall 'Whale' tenant is a fictional stand-in for this kind of deal.
realAnchor: Meta's Hyperion data center campus, Richland Parish, Louisiana

title: The famous exception: rent that starts on schedule anyway
body: Lawyers who structure these deals note a real shift: some investment-grade tenants now agree to start paying rent on a fixed date no matter what caused a construction delay, instead of only after delivery. That one clause is often what lets lenders treat the lease like a bond. In the game, this is the rare lease term players hope their Whale will agree to.
realAnchor: Date-certain rent commencement clauses in hyperscaler data center leases

title: The bond behind the campus
body: To fund a Louisiana AI campus like this, a special-purpose entity issued over $27 billion in senior secured notes in a single offering, with large asset managers anchoring the deal. The notes amortize over roughly 25 years, treating the tenant's occupancy like rent on a very long mortgage. The game's senior loan and takeout mechanics are modeled loosely on structures like this.
realAnchor: Beignet Investor LLC $27.294B senior secured note offering for the Hyperion campus

title: The joint venture that owns the dirt
body: Rather than build the campus on its own balance sheet, the tenant formed a joint venture with an asset management firm, which holds the larger ownership stake while the tenant keeps a minority share and the lease. This keeps most of the debt off the tenant's own books. The game's capital stack and equity split are inspired by this kind of structure.
realAnchor: Meta / Blue Owl Capital joint venture for the Hyperion data center

title: Why air permits matter so much
body: Before a utility can run new gas-fired power plants to feed a campus like this, the state's environmental regulator has to issue air operating and pollution-control permits, and hold public hearings on them. Advocacy groups and residents can and do show up to those hearings to push back on projected emissions. In the game, the air permit is one of the three permits players may need before power can flow.
realAnchor: Louisiana DEQ air permit review for Entergy gas plants serving the Meta campus

title: The first docket vote
body: A real state utility commission voted 4 to 1 to approve a settlement letting the local utility build new generation and transmission to serve a single large tech customer. One commissioner dissented. The game's docket and intervenor mechanics are built around a vote exactly like this one.
realAnchor: Louisiana Public Service Commission Docket No. U-37425 settlement vote, August 2025

title: The expansion docket
body: Less than a year after the first approval, the same commission voted again, this time to fast-track review of a roughly $21 billion follow-on plan for even more generation tied to the same campus. The game's 'the Ask' event, where a tenant requests more halls mid-game and forces a second docket fight, is modeled on this kind of sequence.
realAnchor: Louisiana PSC fast-track vote on Entergy's follow-on generation plan, April 2026

title: Why transformers take years, not months
body: Large power transformers that once shipped in under a year now have published lead times stretching past three years, driven by a global crunch on electrical steel, copper, and factory capacity. Developers who don't order early in a project can find their whole schedule hostage to a transformer they haven't received yet. This is exactly what the game's 'order transformer' action and slip events represent.
realAnchor: U.S. power transformer supply shortage and multi-year lead times, 2025 to 2026

title: The other long-lead item: switchgear
body: Switchgear, the equipment that protects and switches electrical circuits, has seen its own lead times stretch from a few months before the AI data center boom to well over a year, with data-center-grade medium-voltage gear sometimes taking two to three years. Shortages here, alongside transformers, are a leading reason real projects slip their delivery dates.
realAnchor: Switchgear lead-time extensions tied to the data center construction boom

title: The electrician shortage
body: Electrical work makes up a large share of a data center's construction cost, and the trade is short-staffed nationwide. In hot markets, experienced data center electricians can earn total pay well over $200,000 a year, roughly three to four times a typical electrician's salary. The game's labor effects and crew mechanics reflect how real this bottleneck has become.
realAnchor: Electrician labor shortage and elevated wages in data center construction markets

title: The property tax check
body: A real state industrial property tax exemption can cover up to 80 percent of new investment for up to ten years, with even larger exemptions for the biggest projects, but it requires state board and sometimes gubernatorial approval and is not automatic. Developers have to apply for it like any other permit, and it can be denied or scaled back.
realAnchor: Louisiana Industrial Tax Exemption Program (ITEP) for large capital projects

title: The equipment rebate law
body: A real 2024 state law created a sales and use tax rebate on data center equipment and construction spending, covering half of the tax paid, for projects that meet minimum job and investment thresholds. The rebate runs for decades once approved. The game's capital stack assumes a similar one-time break is available if the player qualifies.
realAnchor: Louisiana House Bill 827 (2024), the data center sales and use tax rebate

title: Why water is a registration, not a permit
body: In the real state this campaign is modeled on, a data center that wants to pump groundwater only has to register its wells and estimated usage with a state agency; it does not need an ongoing permit or usage cap unless regulators declare an emergency for that aquifer. That light-touch rule is a real source of local concern, and is why the game treats water as a one-time registration rather than a recurring fight.
realAnchor: Louisiana's groundwater well registration rule for large industrial users

title: What the rating agencies are watching
body: A major credit rating agency has described the data center sector's outlook as broadly positive but increasingly exposed to permitting fights, grid bottlenecks, and local pushback that can delay projects enough to hurt a deal's credit quality. Separately, one large AI cloud company's debt insurance costs have spiked to levels considered financially distressed, a reminder that not every tenant in this boom is equally creditworthy.
realAnchor: S&P Global Ratings' 2026 digital infrastructure credit outlook, and elevated CoreWeave CDS spreads

title: What build-to-suit really means here
body: In this industry, a build-to-suit lease is signed before the building exists, locking in a tenant's specifications and often a residual value guarantee, long before a shovel hits dirt. That is very different from leasing an existing building, and it is why so much of the risk in this game happens before delivery day.
realAnchor: Build-to-suit hyperscaler data center lease structures

title: Delay insurance at campus scale
body: On real campuses this size, delay-in-start-up insurance limits can run from several hundred million to over a billion dollars, because a single storm or fire that pushes back delivery can cost more in lost rent and debt service than the physical repair itself. It has become one of the most expensive and contested parts of insuring a project like this.
realAnchor: Delay-in-start-up (DSU) insurance limits on large data center campuses

title: Builder's risk, in the real world
body: Builder's risk insurance covers physical damage to a project while it's under construction, like storm or fire damage to a half-built hall, but it does not cover the lost rent that follows. That's why real developers buy it alongside delay-in-start-up coverage, not instead of it, the same pairing the game uses.
realAnchor: Builder's risk coverage as distinct from delay-in-start-up coverage in data center construction

title: How rating agencies actually grade these deals
body: Rating agencies mostly adapted their existing large-loan commercial mortgage frameworks to data centers, before some began publishing dedicated data center asset-backed securities methodologies. The market for rating these deals is still young and evolving fast, which is part of why the game's conversion and takeout tests are deliberately strict.
realAnchor: Rating agency methodologies for data center CMBS and asset-backed securities

title: The rack that changed cooling
body: A real flagship AI server rack from a major chipmaker draws around 120 kilowatts, roughly ten times a typical air-cooled rack from a few years earlier, and needs direct liquid cooling to every chip just to run. That jump in power density is why the game treats liquid cooling as a separate, bigger decision than ordinary air cooling.
realAnchor: Nvidia GB200 NVL72 rack power draw and liquid cooling requirements

title: The depreciation debate behind 'chip generation' events
body: Large cloud companies have stretched how long they say their servers and chips last on the books, from three or four years to five or six, which lowers reported depreciation and raises reported profit. Critics argue the real useful life, especially for the newest AI chips, is much shorter. The game's chip generation event is a nod to that real tension between accounting life and actual obsolescence.
realAnchor: Hyperscaler extensions of server and GPU useful-life assumptions for depreciation

title: Why guaranteed maximum price isn't a guarantee against everything
body: Even under a guaranteed maximum price contract, undocumented scope changes, like a mid-project switch in cooling strategy, are a leading real-world cause of budget blowouts, because the original price was never built to cover them. Disputes over whose fault a given change was can average hundreds of thousands of dollars per project. The game's overrun event and GC choice are built around this exact failure mode.
realAnchor: Scope creep and change-order disputes as a primary cause of GMP construction overruns

title: The developer (you)
body: The developer sponsors the whole project: finds the site, wins the permits, signs the lease, raises the capital stack, and carries every risk nobody else agreed to take. By default that means delivery delay, cost overruns, plant slip, refinancing, rate moves and labor. Sponsors of campuses this size rarely build alone: they form joint ventures with asset managers that supply most of the equity, keeping a minority stake and the lease.
realAnchor: Meta / Blue Owl Capital joint venture for the Hyperion data center - the sponsor-developer structure this game's 'you' is modeled on

title: The general contractor (Foreman Ruth Calder)
body: The general contractor runs the site: crews, schedule, subcontractors, inspections. Under a guaranteed maximum price (GMP) contract it absorbs cost overruns above the cap; under cost-plus they stay with you. The largest US data center contractors in 2025 were HITT Contracting, Holder Construction, DPR Construction, Turner Construction, Whiting-Turner Contracting and Mortenson, per Building Design+Construction's Giants 400 ranking.
realAnchor: HITT, Holder, DPR, Turner, Whiting-Turner and Mortenson top Building Design+Construction's 2025 data center contractor ranking

title: The utility (Priya Natarajan)
body: The utility studies your interconnection, builds the power plants and sets the minimum monthly charge. A higher minimum charge lowers slip odds and moves some plant-slip risk to the utility; plants that end up stranded are usually socialized to ratepayers through rates. Real example: Entergy Louisiana, which won approval for gas plants serving the Hyperion campus in a contested 2025 regulatory docket.
realAnchor: Entergy Louisiana's generation docket serving the Meta campus (Louisiana PSC Docket No. U-37425)

title: The tenant (Jordan Ashe, the Whale)
body: The tenant signs the lease that makes the project financeable: delivery dates, rent, late remedies and the outside date. On the hybrid hall tier the tenant keeps chip-generation obsolescence risk; on air tier some of it shifts to you. Real example: Meta, which leases the Hyperion campus from a joint venture it formed with Blue Owl Capital while keeping a minority ownership stake.
realAnchor: Meta, tenant of the Hyperion data center through its Blue Owl Capital joint venture

title: The construction lender (Marcus Teale)
body: The construction lender funds the senior loan draw by draw, sends its own engineer to check progress before releasing money, freezes draws when something looks wrong, and tests the DSCR covenant at conversion. Real example: JPMorgan, which closed a $7.12 billion construction financing in May 2025 for a 1.2 gigawatt data center campus in Abilene, Texas leased to Oracle.
realAnchor: JPMorgan's $7.12B construction financing for the Abilene, Texas data center campus

title: The insurer
body: The insurer carries what it prices: builder's risk for physical damage during construction, and delay-in-start-up (DSU) cover for lost rent after an insured delay, each above a deductible. Decline the cover and the risk stays with you. Zurich Insurance says the average data center project now carries a value of $3 billion, up from $150 million five years earlier, and warns that a project that is not insurable will not get financed.
realAnchor: Zurich Insurance on data center construction values and insurability (Commercial Risk)

title: The equipment makers
body: Transformer and switchgear makers hold your lead times. Their factories are the bottleneck: a fire or a backlog slips your order, and no contract clause makes a missing transformer arrive sooner. Hitachi Energy, the world's largest transformer maker, said in March 2026 that lead times for large power transformers had passed 30 months amid manufacturing bottlenecks.
realAnchor: Hitachi Energy: large power transformer lead times past 30 months (Nikkei)

title: The ratepayers (Lucia Byrne, counsel)
body: Ratepayers are the utility's ordinary customers. When a utility builds plants for a campus that never uses them, the stranded cost usually lands in everyone's rates, which is why ratepayer advocates intervene in dockets like this one. Real example: the contested Entergy Louisiana docket for the Meta campus, where advocates pressed the question of who pays if the promised load never shows up.
realAnchor: Ratepayer advocates in Louisiana PSC Docket No. U-37425 (Entergy/Meta)

title: The town and county
body: The host community grants permits, abates taxes, supplies water and road extensions, and lives with the traffic, the noise and the wells. It holds the water-availability risk when your cooling choice leans on the local supply, and its goodwill moves with how you treat it. Real example: Richland Parish, Louisiana, the rural host of the Hyperion campus.
realAnchor: Richland Parish, Louisiana, host community of Meta's Hyperion campus

title: The equity partner
body: Your equity partner supplies most of the committed equity and most of the second-guessing. The partner's share decides how much of the final equity value is yours, and a dispute with them slows everything. Real example: Blue Owl Capital, the asset manager holding the larger ownership stake in the Hyperion joint venture.
realAnchor: Blue Owl Capital, majority equity partner in the Hyperion joint venture

title: The commission (Odell and Kwambai)
body: The public utility commission votes on the docket that lets the utility build for your load. Commissioners answer to voters, not to you: testimony, discovery answers and intervenor settlements all move the vote, and a failed vote costs months. Real example: the Louisiana Public Service Commission, which fast-tracked approval of Entergy's $2.1 billion follow-on generation plan for the Meta campus in April 2026.
realAnchor: Louisiana Public Service Commission fast-track vote on Entergy's $2.1B plan, April 2026
